title: Does the Spread Stay the Same?
scopeNote: This keeps the paired plots on a shared axis, and reveals the second one only after the learner has tried to answer the question from the first. The standard-error comparison is kept but moved into the closing explanation, because it is the subtlest part and nothing else depends on it. The sample-size control, the repeated-sampling check on interval coverage and the diagnose-four-plots challenge stay in the longer version, and the page says so.
summary: A regression line through sixty people, and one question: does the scatter around it stay about the same width across the range? The line is then taken out, leaving only the misses, and three groups that produce almost the same slope turn out to look completely different once it is.
learningObjectives: Explain that a regression slope summarises the average relationship in a single number.
Explain why the raw scatter plot makes the pattern of spread hard to judge.
Describe a residual as the vertical distance from a point to the fitted line, centred on zero.
Define homoscedasticity as roughly even residual spread across the range, and heteroscedasticity as spread that changes.
Recognise that a slope can look perfectly ordinary while the residual plot reveals a problem it cannot show.
interactionTypes: a scatter plot with its fitted line, shown on its own first
three neutrally named groups to compare by eye before any labels give the answer away
a one-press reveal that takes the line out and draws the residuals beneath, on a shared axis
live spread figures for each end of the range
an ordinary and a robust standard error, held back until the closing explanation
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Every sample is generated and analysed in the browser and is gone when the page is closed.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. The group switch is a radio group with all three labels permanently visible. The figure description changes with the state of the activity: before the reveal it says the question is not settled by the plot alone, and afterwards it names the shape of the residual band in words, an even band, a wedge or an hourglass, and gives the spread across the left third, the middle and the right third along with both standard errors. No diagnosis therefore depends on judging a scatter by eye. Both panels are titled, both vertical axes are labelled in plain words and ticked, and the zero line is labelled on the figure. A written interpretation appears beneath the tiles and differs by group. The figure scrolls sideways rather than shrinking below legible label sizes on a narrow screen. Changes are announced through a polite live region. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Simulated and illustrative. Sixty fictional observations per run, generated from a true intercept of 22 and a true slope of 0.58. Nothing here is real data.
simulationNotes: Randomness is seeded with mulberry32 and Box-Muller normals. The three groups are named A, B and C rather than by their shapes, because a learner who can read the answer off a radio button has not been asked the question. The robust standard error is HC0, the Eicker-White estimator. IMPORTANT, and recorded because it corrects the usual classroom claim: this activity was first written around the assertion that fanning out wrecks the standard error of the slope. Measured across many seeds it does not, and the theory agrees. The ratio of the robust to the ordinary variance is one plus a term in the covariance between the squared centred predictor and the local error variance. A linear fan makes the error variance quadratic in the predictor, whose component correlated with the symmetric squared deviation is small, so the two standard errors very nearly agree. Widest-at-both-ends puts the extra variance exactly where the squared deviation is largest, so they do not. Predicted ratios for this design are 1.000 for group A, 1.046 for group B and 1.259 for group C. A second correction followed: HC0 is a noisy estimator at sixty people, and on a single sample the two figures can differ by ten per cent with the spread perfectly even, so reporting one sample's comparison as though it characterised the design would teach the wrong thing. The closing note therefore reports the average across two hundred repeats of the design, which is stable, and states plainly how far the single sample on screen sits from it. Group B should not be adjusted to look worse.
readmeTopic: whether the spread around a regression line stays the same across the range, and why the residual plot is the only way to see it
